newsitem.title: CANADA: Royal Bank Canada dissident proposals lose.
newsitem.headline: Royal Bank Canada dissident proposals lose.

text.p: Royal Bank of Canada said on Wednesday that proposals by dissident shareholders, including a cap on senior executive salaries and separating the offices of chief executive and chairman, were defeated at the annual meeting.
Shareholders voted separately on each of the four proposals, submitted by Quebec shareholder activist Yves Michaud.
A proposal to limit pay for the bank's top officer to 20 times the average employee salary was rejected by an 89 percent margin.
Shareholders voted 78 percent against and 17 percent in favor of a plan to separate the positions of chairman and chief executive. Nearly five percent of the shares did not vote on the motion.

The final two proposals were both defeated by an 88 percent margin. The first would have made anyone who provides to services to the bank ineligible to become a director and the other would have limited directors' terms to 10 years.
Royal Bank's management had recommended shareholders vote against all four motions.
Bob Verdun, an Ontario newspaper editor, presented the proposals on Michaud's behalf and said the effort was a precedent-setting bid to strengthen shareholder rights in Canada.
"It a beginning of the process....I expected this kind of reaction. But I planted some seeds today," Verdun told reporters after the motions were defeated.

He said the shareholder activists would continue to press the banks to be more accountable. Michaud got proposals on the proxies for both the Royal Bank and National Bank of Canada annual meetings after a court battle. The Royal Bank meeting today was the first chance for shareholders to vote on the ideas.
At the meeting, three other shareholders spoke against the pay cap proposal while one shareholder voiced support.

The meeting turned into a marathon affair lasting more than three hours as Verdun pressed chief executive John Cleghorn and other executives with questions about the bank's practices and comments on the shareholder proposals.

The activist touched on everything from the history of Canada's Bank Act, Royal's sovereign lending, the deposit reserve system, international capital requirements and the value of Royal's mortgage lending business to a complaint that the page numbers in the bank's annual report were too small.
Cleghorn bore the onslaught patiently but drew hearty applause and laughter when he sought on occasion to keep the meeting moving along.
